`git rebase --onto` lets you choose a new base for a range of commits. A plain `git rebase` assumes "my commits are everything since I forked from upstream", but with `--onto` you say which commits to move and where to put them.

## Syntax

```
git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>]
```

Git takes the commits that are in `<branch>` but not in `<upstream>` (the range `upstream..branch`), replays them on top of `<newbase>`, and then points `<branch>` at the result. If you leave out `<branch>`, it uses the current branch.

## Example: move a branch off another feature branch

You branched `feature-b` off `feature-a`, but `feature-b` doesn't depend on `feature-a`'s work. You want it based directly on `main`:

```
main:       A---B
                 \
feature-a:        C---D
                       \
feature-b:              E---F
```

```bash
git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b
```

This means: take the commits in `feature-b` that aren't in `feature-a` (E and F) and replay them onto `main`.

```
main:       A---B
                |\
feature-a:      | C---D
                 \
feature-b:        E'---F'
```

C and D stay on `feature-a` only. `feature-b` now holds just its own work. E' and F' are new commits with new hashes.

## Other common uses

- **Delete commits from the middle of a branch:**
  `git rebase --onto HEAD~3 HEAD~1` drops the two commits `HEAD~2` and `HEAD~1`, and keeps the newest one on top.
- **After the base branch was squash-merged or rewritten:**
  `git rebase --onto main <old-base-sha>` replays only your own commits, so you don't get conflicts from re-applying the old base's commits.

## Caveats

- This rewrites history. If the branch has already been pushed, you'll need `git push --force-with-lease`, and you should let anyone else using the branch know.
- If something goes wrong, `git rebase --abort` cancels a rebase that's still in progress. After it has finished, `git reflog` shows the old branch tip so you can reset back to it.
